channel.title: Security + Policy + Governance News Aggregator
channel.description: Curated Security, Cybersecurity Policy, and Governance news from trusted international sources

item.title: Spain, Denmark and the Netherlands win Europol 2026 Excellence Awards in Innovation
item.description: At the European Police Chiefs Convention on 29 September 2026, Europol announced the winners of its 2026 Excellence Awards in Innovation. Law enforcement teams from Spain, Denmark and the Netherlands took home awards for projects that put innovation to work.

item.title: Teenager suspected of leading KillSec ransomware group as law enforcement seizes servers and leak site
item.description: On 30 September 2026, law enforcement took control of KillSec’s leak site, securing at least 110 terabytes of data against further unauthorised access. The cybercrime group used the site to threaten organisations with the publication of stolen files unless they paid a ransom.

item.title: Cannabis smuggling from North America and Thailand into Europe: Europol highlights growing threat
item.description: Cannabis smuggling from North America and Thailand in Europe has seen a sharp rise, driven by oversupply in legal markets and the adaptability of organised crime groups. A dedicated Europol Operational Taskforce (OTF) has been established to dismantle the criminal networks behind this evolving threat.

item.title: Protecting citizens, preserving rights
item.description:
How can law enforcement make effective use of data and technology while ensuring that fundamental rights and the rule of law remain protected?
This question was at the heart of the 17th Europol Data Protection Experts Network (EDEN) conference, held in Lisbon, Portugal, on 22 and 23 September 2026 under the theme ‘Do Not Cross: Protecting Citizens, Preserving Rights’.

item.title: European and Ecuadorian cooperation leads to 20 arrests in major hit against drug trafficking

item.title: Six arrests for smuggling migrants via Schengen airports
item.description:
Europol supported a migrant smuggling investigation involving law enforcement authorities from 17 countries. The criminal network was also engaged in document fraud and money laundering.
The action day on 22 September 2026 in Austria, Italy, Spain, and the United Kingdom (UK) led to six arrests, 10 house searches, and multiple seizures, including ID documents, electronic equipment, evidence, and a large amount of cash.

item.title: Ordering violence from abroad: five suspects arrested in Spain, Morocco, and France
item.description:
Five suspects linked to the organisation and recruitment of serious violence have been arrested in Spain, Morocco, and France, in the latest results of the Operational Taskforce (OTF) GRIMM, coordinated by Europol.
The arrests in August and September target the upper levels of violence-as-a-service: those suspected of ordering attacks, finding perpetrators and coordinating crimes from abroad. Among those apprehended are fugitives featured on the EU Most Wanted website.

item.title: Android security advisory – October 2026 monthly rollup (AV26-1003)
The 7 biggest issues CISOs and security teams face today
item.description:
Year after year CISOs see the volume, velocity, and sophistication of attacks increase. They also see their attack surfaces expand and increase in complexity.

Advances in artificial intelligence and the rapid growth of AI use in business are also impacting the security agenda, introducing novel attacks, broadening the attack surface to include AI infrastructure, and presenting governance and security control challenges and complications — especially as agentic systems come online.

As a result, 68% of security leaders report that their roles have become more stressful over the past five years, according to the 2026 State of Cybersecurity survey from ISACA, with 71% of CISOs citing the increasingly complex threat landscape as their main stressor, up from 63% in 2025.

Moreover, the introduction of Mythos-class AI models has 50% of CISOs considering exiting the profession entirely, according to a recent survey from Absolute.

To tackle this increasingly complex and intense security environment, security leaders must sharpen their strategies — and their teams’ skills — around the most pressing issues they and their CISO colleagues are facing today.

To help with that, we spoke with security chiefs and cyber experts to identify the seven biggest issues CISOs need to address, with insights on how to tackle the challenges.

1. Preventing compromise — with increased emphasis on resilience and recovery

Although CISOs are increasingly taking on governance responsibilities and business risk mandates, broadening their remit, Kyle McMillan, chief cybersecurity officer at Siemens USA, says all the work in the security organization is still “framed in the context of preventing a compromise.”

It’s a monumental task, McMillan says, as there’s no one formula for the right defense that will work for every CISO. Rather, CISOs must know the specific risk profile of their organizations, the specifics of their IT environment, and the general threat landscape, as well as any threats particular to their industry — and then use all that to formulate a unique plan of defense based on the resources available.

“And there are always trade-offs to be made,” McMillan adds.

While it’s true that thwarting attacks as much as possible and minimizing the damage in the event of a successful breach has always been job No. 1 for CISOs, research shows it’s one they continue to struggle with. The State of Incident Response Readiness, a 2026 report from security software maker Sygnia, found that 73% of CISOs weren’t fully ready for a major cyberattack.

That — and the rise of AI-assisted attack volumes and speed — is contributing to a mindset shift from prevention to resilience. Yes, prevention remains job No. 1, but ensuring business continuity and resilience in the event of an incident is becoming a key emphasis and addition to CISOs’ playbooks. That means honing incident response plans, conducting more relevant tabletop exercises, and sharpening team operations to accelerate cyber recovery.

According to Foundry’s forthcoming Security Priorities Study, 69% of security leaders are currently undertaking this shift.

2. Leading a security program aligned with the organization’s specific needs

One of the biggest issues CISOs continue to face is accurately assessing their organization’s processes, infrastructure, and risk profile and then building a program tailored to their unique security requirements, says Ira Winkler, veteran cybersecurity leader and now CEO and program director of CruiseCon, which offers professional education for security leaders.

“CISOs are not monoliths,” Winkler points out. Some CISOs struggle to patch all the critical vulnerabilities in their environments fast enough, whereas others struggle to tackle essential work with the staff and budgets they have; still others find themselves falling short in taking a strategic approach to their role.

What this often boils down to is a leadership issue. Setting the right security strategy aligned to your specific business, managing resources well, and ensuring teams can execute on the details remain key leadership skills security leaders must develop — both for themselves and their deputies.

For Winkler, this is evidenced by the systems, processes, and controls a CISO puts in place and how well those help the organization as a whole respond to change.

“The quality of a CISO depends on the quality of the systems they put in place on a daily basis,” he says, adhering to the adage that a good cyber security program is like a ship, in that the CISO must build a program capable of sailing forward and staying afloat regardless of the issues that arise.

“You’re always going to deal with something; there’s always something happening,” he says, “so the question is do you have a system in place so that it’s just a little wave pushing you off course or do you not have it in place and it’s going to feel like a large wave? Good CISOs understand the processes they manage and understand what type of operational and technical tools can secure those processes with the resources they have.”

Winkler says CISOs who build seaworthy ships capable of navigating even without a captain on the bridge are at the top of their game.

3. Rethinking cybersecurity for the AI era

To defend against the rise of AI-fueled attacks, CISOs must now design a security program capable of effectively using AI. Alex Levy, CISO of BNSF Railway and the inaugural TIME + Commvault CISO of the Year, lists that as one of the most consequential issues for security leaders today.

Levy is creating a security program for a world where hackers of even moderate skills can use AI to launch the types of sophisticated attacks previously created and executed only by highly resourced nation-state actors. And, Levy notes, his security program must be able to respond to attacks that can be created and launched at a staggeringly fast pace, thanks to AI.

That has put the pressure on him and other CISOs to integrate AI into their security departments, to help speed and scale their capacity to fight these AI-enabled attacks. That includes not only embracing the tools but also preparing teams to collaborate with agentic AI.

Marty Barrack, CISO and chief legal and compliance officer at healthcare IT company XiFin, sees the rise of AI forcing CISOs to rethink the full gamut of their security strategies.

“AI is affecting security on so many different levels that it has made the CISO job a very difficult job,” says Barrack, who is also a member of the ISACA Emerging Trends Working Group. “That is really driving how CISOs think about patching and end of life and thinking about automation and using tools and prioritizing. It’s a totally different environment now. You can’t do things the way you did one, two, three years ago. We ask about any repetition task how we can automate it or reduce the burden on the team while getting the business risk addressed.”

4. Securing AI use and AI infrastructure

Doug Kersten, CISO of tech company Appfire, points out another key issue he is facing: securing the AI increasingly being deployed by his company.

The vast majority of CISOs are in the same boat. According to the Proofpoint’s 2026 Voice of the CISO report, 78% of global CISOs believe generative AI use is a security risk to their organization and 88% list enabling the safe use of AI assistants, copilots, and automation technologies as a top priority for the next two years.

Kersten is collaborating with his company’s AI council, the chief legal officer, head of IT operations, and the engineering team to ensure the AI governance policies set by leadership are followed throughout the organization. Together, they’ve also appointed AI leads in every department to train their colleagues on governance and to ensure that any new AI tools used within their departments fall within the approved safe use standards and guidelines set by security.

Kersten also monitors for unauthorized use of AI, which CISOs also cite as a big issue, with 68% of CISOs having found unauthorized AI use in their organization, according to the Okta’s Global CISO Insights 2026 report.

Moreover, CISOs need to strategize how to secure their organizations’ AI operations and AI infrastructure, including the very tricky task of securing and controlling AI agents. To protect these newer, growing attack surfaces, 43% of CISOs report increasing their investment in AI security posture management (AI-SPM) tools, topping Foundry’s Security Priorities list, with 34% of CISOs also saying that securing agentic AI is a key area their teams need to develop greater expertise with over the next 12 months, No. 2 to cloud security.

5. Addressing skills gaps — for today and tomorrow

Speaking of expertise, another top issue for CISOs is ensuring their teams have the skills needed to secure the organization now and into the future.

“The first issue I would put on the table is whether security teams have the skills and capacity to do everything being asked of them. A CISO can have a talented team and still face a serious gap in a particular area, whether that is cloud security, AI security, risk assessment, or responding to a new kind of attack,” says Casey Marks, COO of ISC2.

He points to ISC2’s 2025 Cybersecurity Workforce Study, which found that 95% of security professionals reported at least one cybersecurity skill need.

Meanwhile, the ISACA survey found that 58% of organizations believed their cybersecurity team is understaffed, up from 55% in 2025. And cybersecurity leaders reported skills gaps among their team, including in soft skills (57%), LLM SecOps (45%), cloud computing (31%), data security (31%), and ML SecOps (31%).

McMillan says the only way he can execute his security strategy is by having a workforce equipped with the necessary skills. He admits he’d “love to hire a stable of cybersecurity unicorns, people who are well suited to everything they lay their hands to, but they don’t exist.” Instead, he hires people who can “grow and develop as fast as the market evolves” and have a solid tech background, understand the company and what it does, and have strong interpersonal skills.

McMillan also works to create an environment where people can grow and develop to ensure staffers can upskill as needed. “A large part of my day to day is spent trying to create these spaces for teams and individuals to have [learning] exchanges and opportunities,” he adds.

The ISACA survey found that to build and maintain their teams, 68% of cybersecurity leaders said they’re offering cybersecurity team members professional development training (up from 60% last year), paying for certification fees (61%, up from 54% in 2025), and paying for certification maintenance fees (59%, up from 52%).

6. Establishing agile security practices and teams to keep pace

The pace of security today is another top issue for security leaders and their teams. The velocity of attacks, the increasingly shorter required response time, and rapidly evolving IT landscape all put pressure on security pros to move ever faster, says Jenai Marinkovic, CISO/CTO for Tiro Security and a member of the ISACA Emerging Trends Working Group.

“The entire incident response process has been turned on its head,” she says. “We no longer have hours to respond. AI-driven attacks are happening sub five minutes, where they can get in, identify the one place in the environment they can exploit, find where it’s not backed up, and execute a ransomware attack.”

Barrack also cites the need for security to move increasingly faster all the time as one of the biggest issues the profession faces today.

“Month to month, companies come out with new direction, new tools, new functions, and new features that have to be considered by security. There are so many innovations, and you just have to keep up. It takes a personal commitment and good prioritization processes and skilled people on your team,” he says.

7. Being flawless at the fundamentals

While AI is transforming everything, including how enterprise security teams operate, CISOs can’t let up on any of the longstanding fundamental practices that form the foundation of the security function.

“It’s easy to chase the shiny new object, and there will always be a shiny new object in cybersecurity, but you can’t fall off those basic principles,” says Grant Yacomeni, CISO at tech company Gigamon. “That includes vulnerability management, identity management, cryptography, supply chain management, endpoint protection. Those basic foundational tasks remain important.”

Yacomeni acknowledges that being flawless at the fundamentals — a longstanding core tenet in cybersecurity — is tough. “It’s not easy. Cybersecurity is not an easy career field, it’s not an easy job,” he says.

To ensure he gets the fundamentals right, Yacomeni leans on prioritizing work and building processes, using his Lean Six Sigman skills (he’s a Green Belt) to succeed in those tasks.

“I don’t like firefighting. I don’t want a simple thing to become a massive thing,” he explains. “But it is easier to say that than do it. So developing processes and people [is critical]. You have to lay the foundation with talented, passionate people who want to be there, processes, policies and measuring your effectiveness. And even if your [security function is] mature, the organization and the threat landscape are always changing, so you have to always be making micro-adjustments and improving over time.”

item.title: These ARE the droids you’re looking for
item.description:
There’s an old leadership fantasy that goes something like this: The CISO surveys a sprawling technology estate, discovers 11 tools doing the work of four, calculates the licensing savings, selects a shiny new strategic platform and declares that consolidation has begun. Six months later, all 11 tools are still running. The new platform is now number 12.

I’ve seen variations of this throughout my career, from financial services to media to technology companies. At CME Group, I eventually gave myself an unofficial title: chief decommissioning officer. The job was considerably less glamorous than the acronym suggested. I had to find technology that had overstayed its welcome, identify who believed they still owned it, determine who actually depended on it and, occasionally, put a bullet in its head.

Buying technology is easy. Killing technology is hard. Tool sprawl is rarely just a technology problem but rather an organizational psychology problem. The industry’s solution has traditionally been consolidation. Buy a platform. Standardize the stack. Reduce vendors and centralize procurement. While all sensible ideas, consolidation efforts routinely stall somewhere between the PowerPoint slide and production.

Why? Because changing the toolset is easy. Whereas changing mindset is far more difficult.

You cannot Jedi mind trick an engineering team

Executives like what is called the “message from the top.” The CEO says security matters. The CIO says everyone will standardize. The CISO announces the strategic platform. Procurement renegotiates contracts. Meanwhile, Gartner produces a quadrant that reassures everybody that the chosen vendor inhabits the correct geometric region. All is well in the world of golf course nepotism.

Then reality arrives. A developer says the new scanner takes 12 minutes longer. A marketing manager has a revenue-generating legacy API they depend on. Exception requests have been filed for several years to allow this tool to continue to exist despite the packages supporting it being end-of-life and receiving no security updates. This is where the “message from the middle” matters.

Transformation does not happen exclusively in boardrooms and fusion teams. It happens in the layer of engineering managers, architects, product owners, security engineers and operations leaders who determine whether the policy announced upstairs becomes the behavior practiced downstairs. Every layer of the org chart is ostensibly trying to do the right thing and make things better. But top-down politics and bottom-up initiatives seldom find one another standing on common ground.

Ignore the middle layer of the org chart and your consolidation project becomes a rather expensive exercise in shelfware. This is something I learned working in European organizations, where consensus building carries more organizational weight than the command-and-control instincts common in American corporations (the Nike-inspired management philosophy of “Just Do It!”). You may have the authority to make a decision without possessing the organizational permission (or “rubber meets the road” context) required to make it stick or worthy of implementation.

Good chief decommissioning officers need a mixture of Jedi and Machiavellian skills. We need persuasion, coalition building, incentives, selective pressure and occasionally the ability to convince people that the idea you desperately need them to support was their idea all along. These are, in fact, the droids you’re looking for.

Every tool comes with an identity

The Star Wars metaphor becomes more useful when we stop thinking of security products as software. Modern security tools have volition and intent. They have:

  • API keys
  • Service accounts
  • OAuth grants
  • Cloud permissions
  • GitHub access tokens
  • CI/CD integrations
  • Slack bots
  • Webhooks
  • Database credentials
  • Kubernetes roles
  • Machine identities and,

increasingly, AI agents are acting with pervasive and persistent delegated human authority.

Every time we introduce security products, we birth another highly privileged account. The industry talks endlessly about human identity. Who is this person and what are they allowed to access? We are decidedly much less disciplined about delegated identity. What is this application allowed to do on behalf of Mike? What is this scanner allowed to read from GitHub? What repositories can this integration modify? Which credentials did we give the old vendor three years ago? And the increasingly important question: when an autonomous agent acts, whose authority is it actually exercising? This changes the economics of tool sprawl. The cost of the twelfth security tool is not merely another annual subscription. It is another (potentially misbegotten) trust relationship.

This is why I’m advocating decommissioning as a core security discipline. Technology organizations suffer from an immortality bias. I gave a “Top-Rated Session” on this topic at RSAC in the spring. We have sophisticated processes for creating things and surprisingly primitive processes for making them disappear. The software development lifecycle is usually illustrated as planning, design, development, testing and deployment. The diagram often ends there, as if every application ever deployed subsequently lives happily ever after. It does not.

Consolidation without decommissioning is multiplication

I’m skeptical when vendors promise “platformization” will solve tool sprawl by itself. A platform strategy can absolutely make sense. Fewer vendors can mean lower licensing costs, fewer integrations and consistent data with less operational complexity. But purchasing a platform does not consolidate anything by itself. Removing the old systems does. That sounds obvious, yet many organizations measure successful consolidation by contracts signed rather than systems eliminated.

Imagine replacing three tools with one platform but leaving all three products technically operational “temporarily.” The service accounts remain. Someone still logs into them. Congratulations! You’ve not consolidated four tools into one but instead consolidated three tools into four. This distinction becomes important as security products gain autonomous capabilities. Yesterday’s forgotten dashboard becomes tomorrow’s forgotten agent with permission to take actions. A zombie application is bad enough, but a zombie application with agency is worse.

Ask the people who actually use the droids

The antidote is not stronger central control but rather explicit ownership. RACI matrix much? Before replacing a tool, find the people who use it and ask an embarrassingly simple question: “What do you actually use this for?” Don’t ask what the contract says. Don’t trust what the architecture diagram might show (*do* check the last modified date, though).

Take what the vendor’s customer-success representative believes with a grain of salt and more than a modicum of skepticism. What do people actually do with it on Tuesday morning? Security leaders are usually surprised by the answer. Maybe the vulnerability scanner’s primary value is not vulnerability scanning. Perhaps an engineering team depends on an obscure export function for its weekly metrics. Maybe the old SIEM has one correlation rule tied to a regulatory requirement that hasn’t been migrated. You will find these things if you look.

This is where the middle of the organization becomes your real intelligence network. The people closest to the systems know where the undocumented dependencies live. Treated as obstacles and they’ll defend their tools. But allow them to be participants and they’ll help dismantle them. A good perspective when planning to kill someone’s baby is to help them understand that they fell in love with the control the tool gave them over the chaos that reigned before it was implemented. And that a new tool can be equally comfortable and easier to support than the burden of the care and feeding that most “heritage” (I prefer this term to “legacy”) applications and solutions require.

Ownership should include the power to recommend retirement. One of the healthiest metrics an organization could create: number of tools and integrations it successfully eliminated this year. We celebrate deployment. Why don’t we celebrate deletion?

The CISO as chief decommissioning officer

Every CISO needs to spend time as CDO. Not chief data officer. Chief decommissioning officer. The role requires asking uncomfortable questions because almost every incentive in technology encourages addition. Nobody gets a press release or a promotion for turning something off. But resilience is partly subtractive.

Every redundant vendor removed is one less company holding your data and one less administrative console an attacker can target and breach. Our industry spends billions asking, “What else should we deploy?” Mature organizations also ask, “What can we safely eliminate?” That second question becomes much more important with agentic AI.

We’re rapidly filling enterprises with digital droids acting on behalf of humans. Regardless of function, almost all require credentials and delegated authority. Organizations that manage this transition successfully will not merely know how to authorize these identities; they will rotate and revoke them automatically. Leadership therefore needs both a message from the top and a message from the middle. The top establishes direction and the middle supplies reality.

Bring the people doing the work into the decision. Make sure your fusion team tasked with consolidating 77 dashboards is comprised of old guard leaders as well as young blood new hires. Strive to understand the dependencies, functional requirements (antiquated as they may be) and non-functional requirements such as availability, integrity and confidentiality. Define what successful retirement looks like before buying the replacement.

Don’t ‘move along’

The next time someone arrives with a miraculous new platform promising to eliminate half of your stack, resist the urge to wave your hand and say, “These aren’t the droids we’re looking for.” They may well be. But before buying more droids, find out who owns the ones already wandering around your Death Star. Find them. Name them. Understand what authority you gave them. And when their mission is finished, dare to switch them off. Create a technology graveyard on your wiki, Confluence or SharePoint site and celebrate the addition of decommissioned tools and technologies with even more fervor than those which have just recently sprung into existence.
